<meta>continues from previous page: ...owing to the peaceful sex. France? Look and take pity. Even now, the gangrene of bloody war creeps through all its joints. And it is no different in the entire world. Think on these things, Lipsius, and by this communion of miseries, lighten your own. And just as it was the custom for a servant to stand behind those celebrating a triumph, who would cry out repeatedly in the midst of the joy of the triumph, **You are a man**: so let this monitor always stand by you, **These things are human**. For just as labor shared with many becomes lighter, so too does sorrow.</meta>

### CAPVT XXVI.

->*Conclusion of the whole discourse. And a brief admonition to repeat and ruminate upon it.*<-

I HAVE unfolded all my forces and my discourse, Lipsius; and you have what I deemed ought to be said in favor of Constancy against Sorrow. I wish that these things were not only pleasing to you, but also healthy; and that they might not just delight, but rather help you. They will help, however, if you let them sink not just into your ears, but into your mind; and if you do not allow these things to lie there and wither after being heard, like seeds scattered on the surface of the soil. <summary>The author concludes the discourse on Constancy, urging the reader to internalize the lessons presented rather than merely hearing them, and emphasizes that repetition and contemplation are necessary to combat sorrow.</summary>
